case_info.scenario: A 40-year-old male patient presented to a primary care clinic with a 2-month history of a pruritic, nontender irritation at the nasal sills bilaterally after minor trauma that involved scratching his nose after getting fiberglass particles in his nostrils while installing lights in his attic. He was a tobacco smoker but was otherwise healthy, with no known allergies. The primary care physician and consulting dermatologist initially diagnosed cellulitis and allergic rhinitis, and the patient was administered a 5-day course of an antibiotic ointment and, as needed, oral antihistamines. Two months later, the patient was referred to the otolaryngology department, as the nasal irritation progressed into a diffuse, destructive process. On physical examination, there was diffuse, ulcerative thickening of the nasal sills bilaterally, with the right side being more severe than the left (Figure 1A). Noncontrast sinus computed tomography showed nasal septal perforation with heterogeneous opacification in the nasal vestibules, along with patchy opacification of the inferior and middle meatus (Figure 1B). Cultures were negative for 1,3 β-d-glucan, aspergillus, cryptococcus, and syphilis. The patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate was within normal limits, and autoimmune serology results (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) were negative. Urine toxicology screening yielded negative results.
case_info.caption: A, Diffuse, ulcerative thickening of the nasal sills bilaterally, with the right side being more severe than the left. B, Noncontrast sinus computed tomography showed nasal septal perforation with heterogeneous opacification in the nasal vestibules, along with patchy opacification of the inferior and middle meatus.
case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 40-year-old male patient presented to a primary care clinic with a 2-month history of a pruritic, nontender irritation at the nasal sills bilaterally after minor trauma that involved scratching his nose after getting fiberglass particles in his nostrils while installing lights in his attic. He was a tobacco smoker but was otherwise healthy, with no known allergies. The primary care physician and consulting dermatologist initially diagnosed cellulitis and allergic rhinitis, and the patient was administered a 5-day course of an antibiotic ointment and, as needed, oral antihistamines. Two months later, the patient was referred to the otolaryngology department, as the nasal irritation progressed into a diffuse, destructive process. On physical examination, there was diffuse, ulcerative thickening of the nasal sills bilaterally, with the right side being more severe than the left (Figure 1A). Noncontrast sinus computed tomography showed nasal septal perforation with heterogeneous opacification in the nasal vestibules, along with patchy opacification of the inferior and middle meatus (Figure 1B). Cultures were negative for 1,3 β-d-glucan, aspergillus, cryptococcus, and syphilis. The patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate was within normal limits, and autoimmune serology results (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) were negative. Urine toxicology screening yielded negative results.

}

[Role]

[Persona]

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your

worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

case_info.explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.
